imageAlt: Protected data storage with a secure backup shield
title: A backup is only good if you can restore it
summary: A backup that is always connected may be reachable during a ransomware incident. Separate copies and occasional restore tests can make the difference between having a backup and being able to recover.
body: Backups are copies of important data that let you recover after a device failure, accidental deletion or cyber incident. But a backup attached to the same computer, or controlled by the same compromised account, may be exposed to the same problem as the original files.

Keep a separate copy that is offline or protected from routine account access. For a business, that might mean using access controls and a recovery plan that prevent an attacker who compromises a workstation from also deleting backup copies. The right design depends on the environment and the value of the data.

Test recovery before an emergency. Restore a small selection of files, check they open correctly, and make sure someone knows how to perform the process. A successful backup report does not prove that the data can be recovered when you need it.
takeaways: Keep at least one backup copy isolated from everyday device and account access.
Test restoring files instead of relying only on successful backup notifications.
Know who can restore systems and where recovery instructions are kept.
